property_summary: The oracle() getter must return the same address that was set in storage via the initializer; the mutant breaks this by hardcoding address(0), so calling oracle() on the reference contract returns the correct oracle address while the mutant returns address(0).

The oracle() getter must return the same address that was set as the oracle during initialization; the mutant always returns address(0), so asserting that the returned address is the one stored in a known reference slot will fail for the buggy version when they differ, which the fuzzer will discover by varying the initialization parameter.

The oracle getter must return the same contract address that is stored in the oracle storage variable; the mutant returns a hardcoded zero address, violating this invariant when the oracle is initialized with a non-zero address.

The oracle() getter must return the same address that was passed as oracle_ during initialization; the mutant hardcodes address(0), so for any non-zero oracle_ the returned address differs, which the fuzzer will discover by varying the initialization parameter.

For any initialized contract, the oracle() getter must return the same non-zero address that was passed as oracle_ during initialization; the bug always returns address(0), invalidating the invariant when a non-zero address was provided.
The payoffDefinition() getter must return the stored definition from storage; the bug returns a hardcoded PASSTHROUGH/LONG/zero definition regardless of what was initialized.

For any admissible initialization parameters, C.payoffDefinition() must return the exact PayoffDefinition that was passed during initialize(); the bug returns a hardcoded PASSTHROUGH/LONG/zero struct regardless of initialization.
The payoffDefinition() getter must return the stored definition from storage; the bug returns a hardcoded PASSTHROUGH/LONG/zero definition regardless of what was initialized.
The payoffDefinition() getter must return the exact PayoffDefinition that was passed during initialization; the bug returns a hardcoded PASSTHROUGH/LONG/zero struct regardless of initialization.

For any valid ProductInfo used during initialization, calling payoffDefinition() must return the exact PayoffDefinition struct that was provided in that ProductInfo; the bug always returns a hardcoded PASSTHROUGH/LONG/zero struct regardless of the actual initialization data.

The payoffDefinition() view function must return the PayoffDefinition value that was provided during initialization; the buggy version returns an all-zero struct instead, violating the equality between the stored definition and the returned value.

The payoffDefinition() getter must return the same PayoffDefinition struct that was provided during initialization; the buggy version returns an all-zero struct, violating equality between the initializer argument and the getter return.

For any valid PayoffDefinition provided during initialization, the public payoffDefinition() getter must return a struct whose payoffType and payoffDirection match the initializer arguments; the buggy version returns all zero values, violating this equality.

For any valid PayoffDefinition used during initialization, calling payoffDefinition() must not revert and must return a struct that matches the stored definition (the buggy empty function returns all-zero defaults, making payoffType and payoffDirection different from the correct stored values).

The payoffDefinition() getter must return a PayoffDefinition whose payoffType/payoffDirection/data equal the values stored during initialization; the buggy version returns an all-zero struct, violating this for any non-zero input.

For any valid oracle returning a price, currentVersion() must return the transformed price as per payoffDefinition; the buggy version skips the transformation and returns raw oracle data, violating the invariant.

For any valid PayoffDefinition and Oracle that returns non-zero price, the transformed price returned by currentVersion() must equal the result of applying payoffDefinition().transform() to the raw oracle price; the buggy version returns the raw price, violating the transformation.

For any valid oracle and payoff definition, the price returned by currentVersion() must equal the transformed price computed by the payoff definition; the bug returns the raw oracle price, violating the transformation.

For any valid OracleProvider returning a price, C.currentVersion().price must equal payoffDefinition().transform(oracle().currentVersion().price); the mutant returns raw oracle price, violating invariant when payoff transform alters the price.

For any valid oracle and payoff definition, the price returned by currentVersion() must be the transformed price; the buggy version returns the raw oracle price, breaking the transformation invariant.

atVersion must return the price transformed by the payoff definition; the buggy version returns the raw oracle price, so for any oracle version the returned price differs when the payoff definition is not an identity transform.

For any initialized C with a valid payoff definition and oracle, calling atVersion returns a price equal to the payoff definition's transform of the raw oracle price; the buggy version returns the raw price without transformation.

For any initialized C, calling atVersion must return an OracleVersion whose price equals the result of applying the payoffDefinition transform to the raw oracle price; the buggy version returns the raw oracle price without transformation, breaking equality.

For any initialized C, calling atVersion must return an OracleVersion whose price equals the result of applying the payoffDefinition transform to the raw oracle price; the buggy version returns the raw oracle price without transformation.
For any initialized C, the return value of atVersion must equal the payoff-transformed oracle version; the buggy code returns the raw oracle version instead.

The controller() getter of the reference contract returns the address stored during initialization (i.e., a non-zero contract), while the mutant returns address(0); any legitimate deployment sets a non-zero controller, so calling controller() must not return address(0) in the reference but always returns address(0) in the mutant.
The reference contract's controller() always returns a non-zero address (the address set during initialization), while the mutant's controller() always returns address(0).

In the reference, controller() returns a non-zero address (the controller set during initialization), while the mutant returns address(0); therefore, any call through controller() that expects a legitimate non-zero contract address will succeed in the reference but may revert in the mutant due to calling address(0).

In the reference, a product initialized through the controller's factory has a non-zero controller address, while the mutant always returns address(0) from controller(), causing any access to controller-dependent functionality to fail.
The controller() view function must return a non-zero address after initialization, but the mutant always returns address(0).

For any non-owner caller that would successfully read the controller address in the correct version, the mutant causes a revert; therefore a read of controller() must not revert for the contract's owner.
